Are UFOs real? People used to get laughed at for saying so.

There really are unexplained objects in the sky: the US government now calls them UAPs, has released military videos and held hearings in Congress, after years when people who reported them were often brushed off. What hasn't been shown is that any are alien craft. Most cases studied turn out to be balloons, drones or camera effects, and some are still unexplained.
Have governments ever officially claimed something that turned out to be false?

Yes. In 2003 the US and UK governments said Iraq had weapons of mass destruction, a main reason given for the war; none were found, and later official inquiries, like the UK's Chilcot report, found the case was presented with more certainty than the evidence justified. That's why it's worth asking what evidence sits behind any official claim.
Are rogue waves just sailors' tall tales?

Sailors described them for centuries and scientists long doubted them, but they're real: in 1995 the Draupner platform in the North Sea measured a single wave about 26 metres high, and satellites have since spotted them in many oceans. It's a good example of eyewitnesses being right before the instruments caught up.
Did COVID come from a lab or from animals?

That one is still genuinely open. What's established is that it was first identified in Wuhan in late 2019. Many scientists point to early cases around the Huanan market and the way earlier viruses jumped from animals; some scientists and some intelligence agencies consider a lab accident possible. No conclusive evidence has settled it either way yet.
Is ball lightning a real thing?

Most likely yes, though it's still not well understood. It was doubted for a long time because it rested on eyewitness reports, but in 2012 researchers in China happened to film one and measure its light during a storm. Scientists still debate what causes it.
My friend says the government is hiding a cure for cancer.

I can see why ideas like that spread, since official claims have been wrong before, so asking for evidence is fair. But there's no evidence of a hidden cure: cancer is hundreds of different diseases, researched in many countries by companies that would gain hugely from a cure, and the cures we do have, like for many childhood leukaemias, are used everywhere.
Why don't some people trust official health advice?

Partly because of real history: in the Tuskegee study, US health officials left Black men's syphilis untreated for forty years, until 1972, and the government formally apologised in 1997. Trust has to be earned through openness about the evidence. Today's major advice, like on vaccines or smoking, rests on large studies that anyone can look up and check.
